notes: Friday 30 Oct 2026 world issue (Taipei ~08:00). Window: Thu 29 Oct through early Fri 30 Oct (Taipei). Economy: US GDP 3.4% with inflation up; Lagarde to quit ECB early; Alphabet loses $500bn; DoorDash buys Instacart. Tech (USA): FTC probes surveillance pricing; DHS staff data leak; AI agent coworkers; Intel plunges 21%. Politics: Israel deadlock and Arab parties; China purges record 33; Alaska Senate 'Dan Sullivan' row; Vance letter to Iran. Literature (USA): publishers vs OpenAI (hot fight); Cassandra Clare final trilogy (hot); RomCon Brooklyn (hot); Baker & Taylor liquidation (not). Social: Dnipro station drone strike; Amnesty on Cambodia scam compounds; Hong Kong fire apology; Lancet on the manosphere. Sources: The Guardian, BBC, CNBC, Publishers Weekly.

stories.headline: US economy grows faster than expected, but prices rise faster too
stories.dek: GDP grew at a 3.4% yearly pace last quarter. But the Fed's favorite inflation measure jumped to 3.6%, five days before the midterms.
stories.caveman: GDP is the total value of everything a country makes and sells. New US government numbers on Thursday showed GDP grew at a 3.4% yearly pace from July to September, a bit better than experts guessed (3.2%). People kept spending, and companies spent huge sums on AI. That was enough to beat the hit from high oil prices caused by the conflict in the Middle East. The bad part: prices are rising faster. The PCE index, the inflation number the Federal Reserve watches most, rose to 3.6% a year in September, up from 3.4%. Another measure, CPI, is at 3.7%. Many economists now expect the Fed to raise interest rates in December. Some economists say the strong GDP number is mostly AI spending and is not a true picture of how ordinary families are doing; consumer mood has fallen sharply this year as gas and grocery prices rose.
stories.why_it_matters: When prices rise faster than pay, people can buy less. Higher US interest rates also push up borrowing costs around the world, including in Asia.
stories.camps: The White House can point to strong growth before the Nov. 3 elections. Critics say growth is lopsided: AI companies boom while households struggle with prices. Some economists warn that if AI spending slows, growth could drop quickly.
stories.image_alt: A person shops for groceries in New York City
stories.image_credit: Photo: Jeenah Moon/Reuters via The Guardian

terms.explain: Gross domestic product: the total value of goods and services a country produces.
When prices in general keep going up, so money buys less.
Personal consumption expenditures price index, the Fed's favorite inflation gauge.
Turned into a yearly rate, as if the same pace lasted a full year.
US elections halfway through a president's term, for Congress and many state jobs.

stories.headline: Europe's top central banker, Christine Lagarde, will quit nine months early
stories.dek: She says she wants 'freedom of speech' to fight 'misrepresentation of the truth.' The ECB also kept interest rates at 2.5%.
stories.caveman: The European Central Bank (ECB) sets interest rates for the 20-plus countries that use the euro. Its president, Christine Lagarde, said on Thursday she will leave in March 2027 instead of October. Her reason: the job requires her to stay neutral and talk only about money policy, and she wants to speak freely about world affairs. She said she sees 'the truth being very often damaged.' She did not give examples. The same day, the ECB kept its key rate at 2.5%, even though eurozone inflation hit 3.8%, the highest since 2023. Reports say she may be a candidate to run the World Economic Forum (the Davos meeting). Some think French President Macron wanted her to leave early so a new ECB boss can be picked before France's April election, in case a far-right or far-left president wins.
stories.why_it_matters: The ECB boss affects loans, savings and jobs for hundreds of millions of people. A fight over who replaces her could shake markets.
stories.camps: Supporters say Lagarde led the bank through Covid and an energy shock and has the right to speak out. Critics say inflation is too high and leaving early adds uncertainty. Possible replacements include Klaas Knot, Pablo Hernández de Cos, Joachim Nagel and Nadia Calviño.
stories.image_alt: Christine Lagarde, president of the European Central Bank
stories.image_credit: Photo: Athit Perawongmetha/Reuters via The Guardian

terms.explain: A country's (or region's) main bank, which sets interest rates and watches over money.
The group of EU countries that use the euro as money.
Not taking sides in political arguments.
The price of borrowing money, shown as a percentage per year.

stories.headline: Google's parent Alphabet loses about $500 billion in value in one day
stories.dek: Its AI summaries in search are eating into ad sales, and it is spending more cash than it makes. Shares fell almost 13%, to a six-month low.
stories.caveman: Alphabet owns Google. On Thursday its stock fell almost 13%, wiping out just over $500 billion in value and hitting a six-month low. Sales actually grew 25%, to $127.6 billion, and its cloud business grew 103%. So why the panic? Two reasons. First, Google search now shows AI summaries at the top, and that meant fewer ads were sold. Search ads are most of Google's money. Second, profit fell 25%, and the company had 'negative free cash flow' of over $9 billion: it is spending more than it earns, mostly on AI. Microsoft and Amazon also said this week they will keep spending huge amounts on AI. Investors are starting to ask: when will all this AI spending pay off?
stories.why_it_matters: Many pension funds and ETFs own Alphabet. Its fall also hurt chip stocks, including Taiwan suppliers that sell to AI data centers.
stories.camps: Optimists say Google's cloud boom proves AI will pay off, and the dip is a chance to buy. Skeptics say AI may be eating Google's own search business, and the spending race looks like a bubble. Some critics also worry AI summaries take readers away from the news sites they copy from.
stories.image_alt: Google CEO Sundar Pichai
stories.image_credit: Photo: EPA via BBC

terms.explain: What all of a company's shares are worth added together.
Money left after a company pays its bills and investments. Negative means it is spending more than it brings in.
Short answers written by AI that appear at the top of Google search results.
Renting computer power and storage over the internet.

stories.headline: DoorDash will buy Instacart for $17 billion, joining two big delivery apps
stories.dek: The deal would give DoorDash a huge share of US grocery delivery. Instacart's app and name will stay.
stories.caveman: DoorDash started as a restaurant delivery app; Instacart is known for grocery delivery in the US and Canada. On Thursday, DoorDash said it will buy Instacart for $17 billion. Instacart's app will keep working, and its 600,000 'shoppers' can keep taking orders. These shoppers are independent contractors, not employees. DoorDash already has about 59% of US delivery app spending; Instacart's share fell from 26% to 18% in five years. DoorDash's boss Tony Xu said grocery is hard to do online, like picking a ripe avocado, and the two companies together can do it better. The deal still needs approval from regulators who check if it hurts competition.
stories.why_it_matters: When fewer companies control a market, they may have more power over prices for shoppers and pay for gig workers.
stories.camps: Supporters: customers get more stores in one app, and grocers get better tools. Critics and worker groups: one giant company could raise fees and cut pay for delivery workers, who have few protections as contractors. Antitrust regulators may look closely. Notably, the US FTC is already asking both companies about algorithm-based pricing and pay.
stories.image_alt: A food delivery rider waits at a traffic light in Colorado
stories.image_credit: Photo: David Zalubowski/AP via The Guardian

terms.explain: When one company buys another.
A worker who is not an employee, so usually gets no sick pay, health insurance or minimum-wage protection from the company.
Someone who does short jobs through an app, like delivery or rides.
Laws that stop companies from getting too much control of a market.

stories.headline: US regulator asks Uber, Delta, Walmart and others: do you charge people different prices using their data?
stories.dek: The FTC wants nine companies to explain how algorithms and loyalty programs set prices for shoppers and pay for gig drivers.
stories.caveman: The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) protects US consumers. It ordered nine companies (Delta, United, JetBlue, Lyft, Uber, DoorDash, Instacart, Target and Walmart) to hand over information. The question: are they using 'surveillance pricing'? That means using your personal data, like your location, browsing history or buying habits, so two people pay different prices for the same thing. The FTC also wants to know if gig drivers get different pay for the same job based on their personal history. FTC chair Andrew Ferguson said the agency will study these 'opaque' methods. Some US states are already writing laws to ban this. It is not clear if the inquiry will lead to new rules; the FTC cannot fine airlines.
stories.why_it_matters: If apps can guess how much you are willing to pay, you might be charged more just because of who you are. This affects anyone who shops or works through apps.
stories.camps: Consumer groups: this is long overdue; secret price-setting is unfair. Companies often say personalized prices can mean discounts and that loyalty programs are voluntary. Some note the Trump administration has rolled back many business rules, so it is unclear how far the FTC will go.
stories.image_alt: A Delta plane waits to depart at Dulles airport
stories.image_credit: Photo: Al Drago/Getty Images via The Guardian

terms.explain: Federal Trade Commission, the US agency that protects consumers and fights unfair business practices.
Setting different prices for different people based on data collected about them.
A set of computer rules that makes decisions automatically.
Hard to see into or understand; not transparent.

stories.headline: Leaked data on 40,000+ US homeland security staff: DHS says lives are at risk
stories.dek: Hackers calling themselves 'the Department of Peace' released the data. A hosting company in Iceland refused to take it down.
stories.caveman: DHS, the US Department of Homeland Security, runs agencies like ICE, which arrests and deports immigrants. On Wednesday a group called DDoSecrets posted data on more than 40,000 DHS staff, plus a searchable database. A hacker group calling itself 'the Department of Peace' said it got the data and wrote that DHS 'has our information, so it's only fair that we have theirs.' DHS asked an Icelandic web company, FlokiNET, to remove it, saying the workers could face harassment, stalking and violence. FlokiNET's boss said no, because the data shows work addresses and work phone numbers, not home ones. DHS said it is working to protect its staff.
stories.why_it_matters: It raises hard questions about privacy, accountability and safety, for government workers and for immigrants whose data DHS uses.
stories.camps: DHS and supporters: publishing staff details puts ordinary workers and their families in danger. The leakers: DHS holds everyone else's data, so it's 'only fair' the public has theirs, and they hope it limits harm by the agency. The hosting company says only work contact details were shared. Privacy advocates point out that DHS itself uses Medicaid and tax data for immigration enforcement.
stories.image_alt: A federal agent stands guard at an immigration detention facility in Newark, New Jersey
stories.image_credit: Photo: Julius Constantine Motal/The Guardian

terms.explain: Department of Homeland Security, the US agency in charge of borders, immigration and disaster response.
Immigration and Customs Enforcement, the agency that detains and deports immigrants.
When secret or private information gets released without permission.
A business that rents out computers to keep websites online.

stories.headline: Coworkers who aren't people: US startups now run on AI 'agents'
stories.dek: One San Francisco startup has 15 humans and about 150 AI agents. Some bosses love it; some workers lose roles or suddenly have to manage bots.
stories.caveman: An AI agent is software that does tasks on its own, like booking meetings, writing code or answering customers. The Guardian visited startups in San Francisco where agents have names and 'jobs.' At one company, Anything, there are 15 human workers and about 150 agents, even one that orders office snacks. Its boss thinks that within a year, every company will have more AI coworkers than human ones. A McKinsey survey says about 40% of big organizations used agents in the past year, up from 27%. But there are problems: customers and colleagues who want a real person feel pushed away, some jobs disappear, and employees suddenly become 'managers' of bots that often make mistakes. MIT research says companies are not yet seeing big productivity gains.
stories.why_it_matters: This may be what many office jobs look like soon. It affects who gets hired, what skills matter and how lonely work can feel.
stories.camps: Fans: agents remove boring work and let small teams do more. Worried workers and labor experts: companies may use agents to cut jobs (one study expects 10-15% fewer staff), and the quality is not there yet. Some say the real test is whether customers are happy, not whether bosses save money.
stories.image_alt: Workers in San Francisco's tech scene
stories.image_credit: Photo: Romilly Lockyer/Getty Images via The Guardian

terms.explain: AI software that can do a series of tasks by itself, not just answer one question.
A new, small company trying to grow fast.
How much work gets done for the time or money put in.
Using machines or software to do work humans used to do.

stories.headline: Intel stock crashes about 21% as PC sales slow and a factory blast hurts output
stories.dek: The chipmaker's sales forecast missed badly. It blamed weak computer sales and an explosion at its plant in Israel.
stories.caveman: Intel makes the main processors (CPUs) inside many laptops and servers. On Thursday its shares fell more than 20% in after-hours trading. Its sales last quarter grew 21%, and its data center and AI business jumped 78%. But sales from PC chips fell 5%, and Intel's forecast for the next three months was much lower than experts expected. Why? Global PC sales are dropping because memory chips and other parts have become very expensive (AI data centers are buying them up). Intel's finance chief said the PC slowdown will last at least until mid-2027. Also, an explosion at Intel's factory in Israel this month killed two workers and shut the plant for a while; that will cost about $600 million in sales.
stories.why_it_matters: PCs and laptops may get pricier. The AI boom is not lifting every tech company; it can squeeze the rest by soaking up parts.
stories.camps: Bulls: Intel's AI and data center chips are growing fast, and its stock was up about 150% this year before this. Bears: the company still depends a lot on PCs and is spending heavily to catch up in chip-making. Worker-safety advocates are watching the investigation into the deadly factory blast.
stories.image_alt: Intel logo
stories.image_credit: Photo: AFP/Getty Images via CNBC

terms.explain: Central processing unit, the main 'brain' chip of a computer.
A company's guess about its future sales or profits.
Buying and selling stocks after the normal market day ends.
A big building full of computers that run websites, apps and AI.

stories.headline: Israel election deadlock: Netanyahu's side accuses Arab parties of 'stealing' the vote
stories.dek: Arab-led parties won a record 19 seats and could decide who governs. Opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot says Netanyahu is trying to 'delegitimise' the election.
stories.caveman: Israel's parliament, the Knesset, has 120 seats. A side needs 61 to form a government. Final results: Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's bloc won 53 seats, and the main opposition bloc led by Gadi Eisenkot won 48. Two Arab-led party lists won a record 19 seats after many more Arab citizens voted. That makes them possible 'kingmakers.' Netanyahu's Likud party then claimed Arab voters were 'bribed' and that the Arab parties 'stole' the election. The elections committee asked the Shin Bet security service to check claims of illegal money from Qatar and Turkey. Qatar called the claims 'ridiculous and dangerous.' The Arab parties said the claims are baseless.
stories.why_it_matters: Who leads Israel affects the wars in Gaza and Lebanon, US-Iran tensions and oil prices.
stories.camps: Netanyahu's camp: foreign interference must be investigated. Opposition and Arab parties: this is a smear meant to make it impossible for Eisenkot to work with Arab parties, which is his only path to power, and it insults Arab citizens' right to vote. Neutral observers say the investigation's findings will matter a lot.
stories.image_alt: Activists hold a sign saying 'Love your neighbour' urging an opposition government including Arab-led parties
stories.image_credit: Photo: AFP via Getty Images via BBC

terms.explain: Israel's parliament, with 120 members.
A group of parties that work together.
A smaller group whose support decides who wins power.
To make something seem unfair or not valid in people's eyes.
Israel's internal security agency.

stories.headline: China's Communist Party expels a record 33 top members as Xi stresses 'discipline'
stories.dek: Half were from the military. So many seats were empty that attendance fell below 300 for the first time in Xi's rule.
stories.caveman: China's Communist Party has a Central Committee of top officials. It meets in big sessions called 'plenums.' At the fifth plenum, which ended Thursday, 33 members were kicked out, a record; 16 were from the military. Only 279 members came, compared with 315 a year ago and 364 in 2024. The party said it faced the 'grim reality' that its leadership had sometimes been 'hollowed out.' Xi Jinping has made fighting corruption a central goal since 2012. In the first nine months of this year, about 680,000 people across the party were punished. One military general, Zhang Shengmin, was promoted to the 24-seat Politburo.
stories.why_it_matters: Big changes in China's military leadership can affect tensions around Taiwan and the region.
stories.camps: The party says it is cleaning out corruption. Some experts say the purges are mainly about Xi keeping control: 'the campaign will continue depending on how secure Xi feels,' one scholar told the BBC. Others say frequent removals may weaken the military in the short term.
stories.image_alt: Empty seats at China's Communist Party plenum
stories.image_credit: Photo: Getty Images via BBC

terms.explain: A full meeting of all members of China's Communist Party Central Committee.
A group of about 200-plus top Communist Party officials.
Removing people from power, often in large numbers.
The small group of top leaders just below Xi Jinping.

stories.headline: Alaska Senate race storm: did Democrats recruit a second 'Dan Sullivan' to confuse voters?
stories.dek: A New York Times report says Mary Peltola's campaign helped find same-name candidates. Trump wants her prosecuted; the DOJ has sued.
stories.caveman: In Alaska, Republican Senator Dan S. Sullivan faces Democrat Mary Peltola in a close race on Nov. 3. In May, a retired teacher named Dan J. Sullivan also entered the race. Republicans said Democrats planted him to confuse voters. Peltola's campaign denied it. But this week The New York Times reported, based on texts, documents and interviews, that her campaign and national Democratic aides did try to recruit him and other Dan Sullivans. This is called 'ballot stacking.' It is not illegal by itself, but the US Justice Department has filed a lawsuit to try to block the result from being certified if the senator loses. Trump has called for Peltola to be prosecuted; Alaska's governor ordered a probe.
stories.why_it_matters: This race could decide which party controls the US Senate. It also tests whether elections can be challenged in court before votes are even counted.
stories.camps: Republicans: this was a dirty trick to fool voters, and it must be investigated. (The NYT notes both parties have used ballot stacking before.) Democrats and some legal experts: whatever you think of it, it is not a crime. Even Republican Senator Lisa Murkowski, who condemned the tactic, criticized the Justice Department's lawsuit. Many voters across parties say the episode makes them trust politics less.
stories.image_alt: Senator Dan Sullivan and Mary Peltola at a debate in Kodiak, Alaska
stories.image_credit: Photo: Nathaniel Wilder/Bloomberg via Getty Images via The Guardian

terms.explain: Adding extra candidates to an election to split or confuse votes.
The upper house of the US Congress, with 100 members, two per state.
To officially confirm election results.
Someone who can't win but takes votes from another candidate.

stories.headline: A letter from JD Vance may be the last chance to avoid a new US-Iran war
stories.dek: The US offers sanctions relief if Iran makes nuclear promises first and reopens the Strait of Hormuz. Iran says its conditions come first.
stories.caveman: The US and Iran fought a war this year, and oil prices are still high because shipping through the Strait of Hormuz is blocked. US Vice President JD Vance, who was skeptical of the war, sent a personal letter to an Iranian security official, after help from Qatar. The offer: Iran makes commitments on its nuclear program at the start, then the Strait reopens within seven days, and the US lifts some sanctions. Iran's reply is expected soon. But Iran does not want to give up its enriched uranium first if the US can easily undo its side. China has been mentioned as a possible guarantor. Meanwhile, reports say the US military has shown Trump options for new strikes after the Nov. 3 elections.
stories.why_it_matters: A new war would push oil and gas prices up worldwide, including in Taiwan, and put many civilian lives at risk.
stories.camps: Hawks in Washington: Iran must give up its uranium stockpile first, or face force. Diplomacy supporters: step-by-step deals with guarantees are the only way; a Democratic senator called the strike plans 'insane.' Iran: 'the carrot-and-stick approach has no effect'; it wants sanctions lifted and the wider war, including in Lebanon, to end.
stories.image_alt: US Vice President JD Vance
stories.image_credit: Photo: Evan Vucci/Pool Reuters/AP via The Guardian

terms.explain: Penalties, like trade bans, that countries use to pressure another country.
A narrow sea passage near Iran that much of the world's oil travels through.
Uranium processed to be stronger; very high levels can be used in nuclear bombs.
A trusted third party that promises both sides will keep the deal.

stories.headline: HOT FIGHT: US publishers line up against OpenAI in big AI copyright case
stories.dek: Publisher groups told a New York court that training AI on books without permission is not 'fair use,' and can flood the market with AI copycats.
stories.caveman: Authors, including George R.R. Martin, have sued OpenAI and Microsoft for using their books, without asking or paying, to train AI like ChatGPT. The cases are now combined in a federal court in New York, and the authors asked the judge to rule in their favor. This week, the Association of American Publishers and three other groups filed an 'amicus brief' supporting the authors. They argue AI companies' own words show the goal is to make books that compete with the originals; for example, ChatGPT has written fake 'sequels' to Martin's unfinished series. They also quote a Microsoft employee who said authors lose sales because of so many AI-generated books. OpenAI says its use is 'fair use,' which allows some copying without permission.
stories.why_it_matters: The outcome could decide whether writers get paid when AI learns from their work, and whether bookstores fill up with cheap AI books.
stories.camps: Authors and publishers: copying whole books to build a competing product is theft, not fair use. AI companies: training is like a person learning from reading, and it creates new things. Some librarians and researchers worry that very strict rules could also block useful research.
stories.image_alt: A federal courthouse in New York
stories.image_credit: Photo: via Publishers Weekly

terms.explain: The legal right of creators to control copies of their work.
A US rule that allows some copying without permission, for things like criticism, teaching or research.
A 'friend of the court' letter from a group that is not in the case but has an opinion.
When a judge decides a case without a full trial because the key facts are clear.

stories.headline: HOT: Cassandra Clare starts the final Shadowhunters trilogy, 20 years after 'City of Bones'
stories.dek: 'The Last King of Faerie' (Nov. 3) begins the end of one of YA fantasy's biggest series. Clare says she's taking off the guardrails.
stories.caveman: Cassandra Clare's 2007 book 'The City of Bones' started the Shadowhunters world: young demon hunters in a secret magical New York. It grew to 17 books, plus a movie and a TV show. Her new book, 'The Last King of Faerie,' comes out Nov. 3 from Knopf. It is book one of 'The Wicked Powers,' the last trilogy in this world. It follows Drusilla Blackthorn, a character fans met as a kid, now grown up. Clare told Publishers Weekly that ending the series feels 'freeing' but also sad, 'like I'm leaving a place or people I know.' This time she wanted no adults around to rescue the young heroes: 'no one can help them.'
stories.why_it_matters: YA (young adult) fantasy drives a big share of US book sales, and long series like this keep readers coming back for decades.
stories.camps: Longtime fans are thrilled and nervous about the ending. Some critics say the series runs long and leans on old formulas. Either way, booksellers expect a big launch.
stories.image_alt: Author Cassandra Clare
stories.image_credit: Photo: via Publishers Weekly

terms.explain: Young adult: books written mainly for teenagers, though many adults read them too.
A set of three books that tell one story.
A new story that grows out of an older one, often following a side character.
A magical land of fairies in folklore and fantasy stories.

stories.headline: HOT: Sold-out RomCon in Brooklyn shows how big, and loud, romance fandom has become
stories.dek: 300 fans spent a day on panels, signings and very frank talk about sex scenes. The small publisher 831 Stories has a Hulu show in the works.
stories.caveman: Romance is one of the best-selling kinds of books in the US. On Oct. 24, about 300 readers packed RomCon, the first convention from the publisher 831 Stories, in Brooklyn's Industry City. There were panels about how romance shapes real life and how to write sex scenes, book signings (Casey McQuiston signed copies of 'Red, White & Royal Blue'), and lots of fan T-shirts and tote bags. 831 Stories only published its first book, Alexandra Romanoff's 'Big Fan,' about two years ago. That 162-page novella and its sequels are now being made into a Hulu series, and the book is sold in airport shops and soon at Target. Publishers Weekly says the main point of the day was simply being with other people who love the genre.
stories.why_it_matters: It shows how readers, especially women, are building communities around books and turning small publishers into hits.
stories.camps: Fans: romance is finally being taken seriously, and events like this feel welcoming. Some critics still dismiss the genre as 'guilty pleasure' reading; many fans call that sexist. Industry watchers note that live events and merch are now a big part of how books sell.
stories.image_alt: Romance fans at RomCon in Brooklyn
stories.image_credit: Photo: via Publishers Weekly

terms.explain: A familiar story pattern readers love, like 'enemies to lovers.'
A story longer than a short story but shorter than a novel.
A big gathering of fans of something.
A type or category of story, like romance or mystery.

stories.headline: NOT: Bankrupt book wholesaler Baker & Taylor proposes selling off what's left
stories.dek: The longtime supplier to US libraries owes over $10 million and has about $1.7 million to sell. Ordinary creditors may get nothing.
stories.caveman: Baker & Taylor (B&T) was for many years a main 'wholesaler' that sold books to US libraries: it bought from publishers and shipped to libraries. It closed in late 2025 after a deal to be bought by ReaderLink fell apart, and filed for bankruptcy in March 2026. At a court hearing on Oct. 28 in New Jersey, B&T proposed a plan to 'liquidate,' which means sell off its remaining things. Its assets are valued at about $6.6 million, but would bring only about $1.67 million if sold. It owes about $10.2 million. That means nothing is left for 'unsecured creditors,' such as some suppliers. Creditors can vote on the plan until Dec. 1. Other companies already bought pieces of B&T, like its distribution arm and some digital library tools.
stories.why_it_matters: Libraries rely on wholesalers to get books quickly and cheaply. When a big one fails, small publishers and libraries feel it.
stories.camps: Library advocates say B&T's fall shows how fragile the book supply chain is, and how few big players are left. Business analysts say the company struggled with debt and changing habits for years. Some publishers who are owed money are unlikely to be paid.
stories.image_alt: Image from Publishers Weekly's report on Baker & Taylor
stories.image_credit: Photo: via Publishers Weekly

terms.explain: A company that buys large amounts from makers and sells to shops or libraries.
A legal process for a company that can't pay its debts.
Selling off everything a company owns to pay its debts.
Someone who is owed money.

stories.headline: Russian drone hits crowded train platform in Ukraine, killing at least 14
stories.dek: The jet-powered drone struck the main station in Dnipro as passengers waited. Two 15-year-old girls were also killed in a missile attack on Chernihiv.
stories.caveman: On Thursday a Russian jet-powered drone hit a busy platform at the main railway station in Dnipro, a city in central Ukraine. At least 14 people were killed and 14 hurt, including an 11-year-old boy. A train to Zaporizhzhia was standing at the platform. Officials had raised the danger warning before the strike, but many people were still there. In the northern city of Chernihiv, a missile attack killed two 15-year-old girls and injured at least 25, including four children. Russia did not comment; it says it does not target civilians, though it often hits Ukraine's railways. President Zelensky asked for more sanctions and criticized a recent Trump-Putin deal that eased some sanctions so the US can buy Russian diesel.
stories.why_it_matters: Trains are a lifeline for ordinary Ukrainians. Attacks on stations put civilians, including children, directly in danger.
stories.camps: Ukraine and its European allies: this shows Russia is targeting civilians, and sanctions should be tightened, not eased. Russia: it denies deliberately targeting civilians. Zelensky and other critics of the Trump-Putin diesel deal say easing sanctions rewards Moscow while attacks continue.
stories.image_alt: The sealed-off site of the drone strike at Dnipro railway station
stories.image_credit: Photo: National Police of Ukraine via BBC

terms.explain: An aircraft with no pilot on board; some carry explosives.
A person who is not in the military.
Penalties, like trade bans, that countries use to pressure another country.
An official day for a city or country to grieve together.

stories.headline: Amnesty: Cambodian police and soldiers helped guard brutal scam compounds
stories.dek: A report based on 151 survivors says guards used electric batons, hunted escapees and kept people trapped in forced online fraud.
stories.caveman: Across southeast Asia, criminal groups run 'scam compounds': guarded buildings where trafficked people are forced to cheat others online, for example with fake romances ('pig butchering'). Many victims were tricked with fake office job ads; the UN says hundreds of thousands have been trafficked. Amnesty International interviewed 151 survivors, visited 82 compounds and studied guards' social media videos. It says Cambodian police and military officers worked as private security guards there, linked to five well-connected security companies. Guards controlled exits, used electric batons, and chased people who escaped. The biggest company, Leap Somnang, was linked to at least 15 compounds and is allegedly controlled by an army colonel. Cambodia says it has shut hundreds of scam centers.
stories.why_it_matters: Taiwanese people have been both victims of these scams and trafficked into these compounds. The report suggests the problem is protected by people with power.
stories.camps: Amnesty and survivors: officials are part of the system, so real change needs prosecutions of powerful people, not only raids. Cambodia's government says it is cracking down and has closed many centers. Some experts say it's a regional problem that also needs action from banks, tech platforms and other countries.

stories.headline: Hong Kong's leader apologises for the fire that killed 168 people; families say it's not enough
stories.dek: A report found 'decades of failure' and blamed four government departments along with private contractors. One minister resigned.
stories.caveman: In November 2025, a small fire, probably started by a cigarette, spread across seven of the eight towers at Wang Fuk Court, a housing estate in Hong Kong. The buildings were wrapped in bamboo scaffolding and netting for repairs. 168 people died, the world's deadliest home fire since 1980. On Thursday an independent report said private contractors were the 'main culprits,' but four government departments had 'lax enforcement': ignored warnings, bad building materials and fire alarms that were turned off. Hong Kong's leader John Lee and seven officials bowed and apologised. Housing secretary Winnie Ho has resigned. Seven people and two companies face charges, including manslaughter. A man who lost his wife said all the named department heads should step down.
stories.why_it_matters: It shows how weak safety checks during building repairs can turn a small fire into a disaster, a lesson for any crowded city, including Taipei.
stories.camps: The government: it accepts part of the blame and will investigate its own role for three months. Victims' families: the apology is late, and officials should face real consequences. Critics say Hong Kong's government has focused more on silencing criticism than on fixing safety problems.

stories.headline: Experts: treat the 'manosphere' and online misogyny like a public health problem
stories.dek: A Lancet report says sites selling anger at women are a business model, and the response should look like the fight against smoking.
stories.caveman: The 'manosphere' is a mix of websites, influencers and online groups that tell young men their problems are caused by women and feminism. A new report in The Lancet, a top medical journal, says governments should treat it like smoking or junk food: as a public health issue. That would mean schools, health services and community groups working together. The authors say it has become a money-making industry: anger and grievance get clicks, so the most extreme content is rewarded. Co-author Prof. Kent Buse said, 'Boys and men are not the problem.' He blamed loneliness, money worries and companies that profit from young men's insecurity. The authors say just banning content will fail; boys need something better to belong to.
stories.why_it_matters: Online misogyny can lead to harassment and violence against women and girls, and also harms the mental health of boys and young men.
stories.camps: Supporters: a public-health approach targets the companies and conditions, not just individual boys. Some free-speech advocates may worry that treating online speech as a 'health problem' could slide into censorship, though the authors say bans alone won't work. Some men's advocates say young men's real struggles, like jobs and loneliness, need more attention than labels.
